silo_relevance: This paper is directly relevant to portfolio_optimization because it studies sector rotation as a sequential allocation problem and evaluates whether quantum-enhanced policies improve portfolio selection and rebalancing outcomes. Its main value for this silo is the head-to-head comparison of quantum and classical policy networks under the same PPO setup, plus the finding that proxy rewards can diverge from actual return and risk-adjusted performance.

key_points.point: Sector rotation is framed as an allocation problem over industry sectors, which maps closely to portfolio selection and rebalancing.
key_points.silo_note: For portfolio_optimization, the core task is choosing how to allocate capital across sectors over time, not just predicting labels.

key_points.point: The paper provides a unified PPO benchmark for comparing classical and quantum policy/value networks on the same portfolio-style decision task.
key_points.silo_note: This is useful for portfolio_optimization because it isolates whether quantum backbones add value to allocation policies under controlled conditions.

key_points.point: The reward function is a proxy based on top-N sector hits and does not directly optimize cumulative return or Sharpe ratio.
key_points.silo_note: This is highly relevant to portfolio_optimization because reward design determines whether the learned allocator actually improves portfolio performance.

key_points.point: Quantum models achieved higher training reward but worse realized portfolio metrics than classical LSTM/Transformer baselines.
key_points.silo_note: For portfolio_optimization, the key question is out-of-sample return, Sharpe ratio, and drawdown; the paper shows quantum reward gains did not translate into better portfolios.

key_points.point: The authors attribute poor quantum portfolio performance to overfitting/instability and suggest better encoding, regularization, and reward shaping as future directions.
key_points.silo_note: This matters for portfolio_optimization because it identifies the main obstacles to making quantum allocation models practically useful.
